authority: tree-sitter grammar sources; every operator is attributed to the grammar rule that admits it

sources.note: inherited from the C base grammar
C++ override adds the alternative-token spellings
the C++ override widens it: `($, original) => choice(original, seq('sizeof','...','(',identifier,')'))`, adding `sizeof...(pack)`
reached through `original` in the C++ override
C++ adds three-way comparison and the alternative tokens
C++ widens the index to a subscript_argument_list (a[i, j])

annex.note: declaration-side operator inventories: spellings the grammar admits when an operator is being DECLARED or listed, not when an expression is being built. Not counted in the arity buckets.

sources.note: the FOLD_OPERATORS table -- the operators that may appear inside a C++17 fold, not standalone expression operators

the spellings that may follow the `operator` keyword in an overload declarator -- a declaration-side inventory, not an expression-side one. `->*` appears HERE and in the fold table but in NO expression rule of tree-sitter-cpp v0.23.4, so `a->*p` has no dedicated node kind in this grammar.

distinctive.and/or/xor/bitand/bitor/compl/not/not_eq: alternative tokens for the punctuation operators

sources.note: seq('&', choice(seq('raw', choice('const', mutable_specifier)), optional(mutable_specifier)), value) -- the raw-reference forms are assembled from separate tokens
prefix arm seq(choice('..','...','..='), expr) -- the grammar writes the choice once and reuses it in three arms
table over the module consts multiplicativeOperators, additiveOperators, comparativeOperators plus '&&' and '||'
assignmentOperators = multiplicative.concat(additive).map(o => o + '=').concat('=') -- built by string concatenation, so the compound spellings never appear as literals in the source

distinctive.&^: bit clear (AND NOT); also &^= in the assignment set

sources.note: '!' arrives as $.bang and '.' as $._dot, both external scanner tokens aliased back to their text form
OPEN SET: $.custom_operator is a scanner-produced token, so user-defined prefix operators are admitted without being enumerated
OPEN SET: seq(lhs, $.custom_operator, rhs). Swift's overflow operators &+ &- &* and every user-defined infix operator go through here; the grammar does NOT enumerate them.
'=' arrives as $._equal_sign -> alias($._eq_custom, '='). NOTE the grammar admits no &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>=, &&=, ||=, ??=
one rule covers both paren call arguments and bracket subscript arguments
prefix arm of the choice(seq(op, arg), seq(arg, op))
seq(condition, '?', optional(consequence), ':', alternative); the optional consequence also admits the GNU `a ?: b`

distinctive.?:: the GNU elided-middle form is admitted (optional consequence)

sources.note: OPEN SET: seq(lhs, $.simple_identifier, rhs). Kotlin's bitwise operations (and, or, xor, shl, shr, ushr, inv) are infix FUNCTIONS and reach the tree through here -- the grammar enumerates no bitwise operator tokens at all.
TS override adds optional type_arguments to the call
'|>' is the PHP 8.5 pipe operator; '.' is string concatenation
seq(condition, '?', optional(body), ':', alternative) -- the optional body is the short ternary `a ?: b`
'<>' is the Python-2 inequality; 'not in'/'is not' arrive as aliased hidden tokens
seq(left, choice(seq('=', right), seq(':', type), seq(':', type, '=', right))) -- the ':' arm is the annotated form
seq(expression, 'if', expression, 'else', expression) -- Python spells its ternary with keywords, not ?:

distinctive.<>: Python-2 inequality, still admitted by the grammar

sources.note: same operator set in command (paren-less) position
'-', '*', '**' arrive as _binary_minus / _binary_star / _binary_star_star aliased back to their text form

annex.note: declaration-side operator inventories: spellings the grammar admits when an operator is being DECLARED or listed, not when an expression is being built. Not counted in the arity buckets.

sources.note: the spellings that may be DEFINED as a method name (`def <op>`) -- a declaration-side inventory, not an expression-side one. `+@`/`-@`/`~@` are the unary forms and `[]`/`[]=` the index read/write forms.
